# Intro

## Intro

- Last lecture: EH failed, forwards forecast returns, Diebold-Li summarized the curve
- Today: build a no-arbitrage model that separates expected rates from term premia
- Goal: move from reduced-form curve dynamics to a structural pricing system
- This is where $\mathbb{P}$, $\mathbb{Q}$, and $\lambda_t$ start doing real work

## Why EH Is Not Enough

- EH was a useful benchmark, but too restrictive
- It ruled out time-varying expected bond returns
- The data did not cooperate [@FamaBliss1987; @CampbellShiller1991]
- We need a model where the whole curve is priced jointly
- And where expected short rates and term premia are different objects

## What This Model Will Deliver

- A state vector $X_t$
- Dynamics under the physical measure $\mathbb{P}$
- An explicit market price of risk $\lambda_t$
- Risk-neutral dynamics under $\mathbb{Q}$
- Bond prices, yields, risk-neutral yields, and term premia

## Flight Plan

- Part I: affine setup under $\mathbb{P}$
- Part II: change of measure and why pricing uses $\mathbb{Q}$
- Part III: exponential-affine bond pricing
- Part IV: risk-neutral yields and term premia
- Part V: implementation and estimation with observed factors only

# Part I: Setup Under $\mathbb{P}$

## State Vector and VAR Under $\mathbb{P}$

- Let $X_t \in \mathbb{R}^K$ collect the term-structure factors
- In this lecture, $X_t$ is *observed*
- Think: first few PCs of yields, or a small set of yields

$$
X_{t+1} = \mu + \Phi X_t + \Sigma \varepsilon_{t+1},
\qquad
\varepsilon_{t+1}\sim N(0,I_K)
$$

- $\mathbb{P}$ is the actual law of motion in the data

## Affine Short Rate

$$
y_t^{(1)} = \delta_0 + \delta_1^\top X_t
$$

- Same notation as last lecture
- The one-period yield is the short rate
- The short end of the curve moves with the state
- Once $X_t$ is given, the short rate is pinned down

## SDF and Market Price of Risk

$$
m_{t+1}
=
- y_t^{(1)}
-\frac12 \lambda_t^\top\lambda_t
-\lambda_t^\top \varepsilon_{t+1}
$$

$$
\lambda_t = \lambda_0 + \lambda_1 X_t
$$

- The SDF comes first: it is the pricing object
- $\lambda_t$ is the market price of risk embedded inside it
- If $\lambda_t$ changes with $X_t$, bond premia change with the state
- No $\Lambda_1$: we use $\lambda_1$

## Economic Interpretation

- $\mathbb{P}$: how the state actually evolves
- $m_{t+1}$: how payoffs are discounted
- $\lambda_t$: how much compensation investors require for bond risk
- If $\lambda_t$ varies with $X_t$, term premia vary with $X_t$
- That is already something EH could not do

# Part II: Change of Measure

## One-Step Density Ratio

Define
$$
\frac{d\mathbb{Q}}{d\mathbb{P}}\Big|_{t+1}
=
\exp\left(
-\frac12 \lambda_t^\top \lambda_t
-\lambda_t^\top \varepsilon_{t+1}
\right)
$$

- This is the one-step Radon-Nikodym derivative
- It tilts probabilities state by state
- We now need to check that this is a valid density
- Notice that it is a positive random variable

## Quick Recall: Gaussian MGF

If $\varepsilon_{t+1}\sim N(0,I_K)$ under $\mathbb{P}$, then for any $a_t$ known at time $t$,
$$
\mathbb E_t^{\mathbb{P}}\!\left[e^{a_t^\top \varepsilon_{t+1}}\right]
=
\exp\left(\frac12 a_t^\top a_t\right)
$$

- We will use this twice
- First to show the density integrates to one
- Then to prove the shifted shock is standard normal under $\mathbb{Q}$

## It Integrates to One

Conditioning on time $t$,
$$
\mathbb E_t^{\mathbb{P}}\!\left[\frac{d\mathbb{Q}}{d\mathbb{P}}\Big|_{t+1}\right]
=
e^{-\frac12 \lambda_t^\top\lambda_t}
\mathbb E_t^{\mathbb{P}}\!\left[e^{-\lambda_t^\top \varepsilon_{t+1}}\right]
$$

Applying the Gaussian mgf with $a_t=-\lambda_t$,
$$
\mathbb E_t^{\mathbb{P}}\!\left[e^{-\lambda_t^\top \varepsilon_{t+1}}\right]
=
\exp\left(\frac12 \lambda_t^\top \lambda_t\right)
$$

so
$$
\mathbb E_t^{\mathbb{P}}\!\left[\frac{d\mathbb{Q}}{d\mathbb{P}}\Big|_{t+1}\right] = 1
$$

## The Shifted Shock

Define
$$
\varepsilon_{t+1}^{\mathbb{Q}} \equiv \varepsilon_{t+1} + \lambda_t
$$

- Under $\mathbb{Q}$, this will become the convenient innovation
- Same state variables, different conditional law
- We now prove explicitly that $\varepsilon_{t+1}^{\mathbb{Q}} \sim N(0,I_K)$ under $\mathbb{Q}$

## Mgf Proof Under $\mathbb{Q}$

For any $u\in \mathbb R^K$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_t^{\mathbb{Q}}\left[e^{u^\top \varepsilon_{t+1}^{\mathbb{Q}}}\right]
&=
\mathbb E_t^{\mathbb{P}}\left[
\frac{d\mathbb{Q}}{d\mathbb{P}}\Big|_{t+1}
e^{u^\top(\varepsilon_{t+1}+\lambda_t)}
\right] \\
&=
\exp\left(
u^\top\lambda_t-\frac12 \lambda_t^\top\lambda_t
\right)
\mathbb E_t^{\mathbb{P}}\left[
e^{(u-\lambda_t)^\top \varepsilon_{t+1}}
\right] \\
&=
\exp\left(
u^\top\lambda_t-\frac12 \lambda_t^\top\lambda_t
+\frac12 (u-\lambda_t)^\top (u-\lambda_t)
\right) \\
&=
\exp\left(\frac12 u^\top u\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

- This is the mgf of $N(0,I_K)$
- So $\varepsilon_{t+1}^{\mathbb{Q}} \sim N(0,I_K)$ under $\mathbb{Q}$

## $\mathbb{Q}$-Dynamics of the State

Start from the $\mathbb{P}$-VAR and replace $\varepsilon_{t+1}=\varepsilon_{t+1}^{\mathbb{Q}}-\lambda_t$:
$$
X_{t+1}
=
\mu + \Phi X_t + \Sigma(\varepsilon_{t+1}^{\mathbb{Q}}-\lambda_t)
$$

Using $\lambda_t=\lambda_0+\lambda_1 X_t$,
$$
X_{t+1}
=
\underbrace{(\mu-\Sigma\lambda_0)}_{\equiv \mu^{\mathbb{Q}}}
+
\underbrace{(\Phi-\Sigma\lambda_1)}_{\equiv \Phi^{\mathbb{Q}}}X_t
+
\Sigma \varepsilon_{t+1}^{\mathbb{Q}}
$$

## Pricing Uses $\mathbb{Q}$, Not $\mathbb{P}$

$$
P_t^{(n+1)} = \mathbb E_t^{\mathbb{P}}[M_{t+1}P_{t+1}^{(n)}]
=
e^{-y_t^{(1)}} \mathbb E_t^{\mathbb{Q}}[P_{t+1}^{(n)}]
$$

- There is a state evolution under both $\mathbb{P}$ and $\mathbb{Q}$
- But the bond pricing recursion uses $\mathbb{Q}$
- $\mathbb{P}$ matters for forecasts and expected excess returns
- $\mathbb{Q}$ matters for prices
- This is not "just different initial conditions": the dynamics themselves change

# Part III: Bond Pricing

## Pricing Equation

For a zero-coupon bond,
$$
P_t^{(n+1)} = \mathbb E_t^{\mathbb{P}}[M_{t+1}P_{t+1}^{(n)}]
=
e^{-y_t^{(1)}} \mathbb E_t^{\mathbb{Q}}[P_{t+1}^{(n)}]
$$

- Last lecture gave the bond math
- Now we impose no arbitrage
- Once we know the short rate and the $\mathbb{Q}$-dynamics, all bond prices are pinned down

## Exponential-Affine Guess

Guess [@DuffieKan1996]
$$
P_t^{(n)} = \exp(A_n + B_n^\top X_t)
$$

with
$$
A_0 = 0,
\qquad
B_0 = 0
$$

- $P_t^{(0)}=1$ is the base case
- The question is whether this functional form closes under the recursion

## Plug the Guess Into the Pricing Equation

Use
$$
y_t^{(1)}=\delta_0+\delta_1^\top X_t
$$
and
$$
X_{t+1}=\mu^{\mathbb{Q}}+\Phi^{\mathbb{Q}} X_t+\Sigma \varepsilon_{t+1}^{\mathbb{Q}}
$$

Then
$$
P_t^{(n+1)}
=
e^{-\delta_0-\delta_1^\top X_t}
\mathbb E_t^{\mathbb{Q}}\left[
\exp\left(
A_n + B_n^\top X_{t+1}
\right)
\right]
$$

## Compute the Gaussian Expectation

Substitute for $X_{t+1}$ and collect what is known at time $t$:
$$
P_t^{(n+1)}
=
e^{-\delta_0-\delta_1^\top X_t}
\mathbb E_t^{\mathbb{Q}}\left[
\exp\left(
A_n + B_n^\top(\mu^{\mathbb{Q}}+\Phi^{\mathbb{Q}}X_t+\Sigma \varepsilon_{t+1}^{\mathbb{Q}})
\right)
\right]
$$

$$
P_t^{(n+1)}
=
\exp\left(
A_n-\delta_0
+B_n^\top \mu^{\mathbb{Q}}
+[(\Phi^{\mathbb{Q}})^\top B_n-\delta_1]^\top X_t
\right)
\mathbb E_t^{\mathbb{Q}}\left[
e^{B_n^\top\Sigma\varepsilon_{t+1}^{\mathbb{Q}}}
\right]
$$

Because $\varepsilon_{t+1}^{\mathbb{Q}}\sim N(0,I_K)$,
$$
\mathbb E_t^{\mathbb{Q}}\left[
e^{B_n^\top\Sigma\varepsilon_{t+1}^{\mathbb{Q}}}
\right]
=
\exp\left(
\frac12 B_n^\top\Sigma\Sigma^\top B_n
\right)
$$

## Affine Recursions

Matching coefficients gives
$$
A_{n+1}
=
A_n + B_n^\top \mu^{\mathbb{Q}}
+ \frac12 B_n^\top \Sigma\Sigma^\top B_n
- \delta_0
$$

$$
B_{n+1}
=
(\Phi^{\mathbb{Q}})^\top B_n - \delta_1
$$

- The recursion closes
- This is why the model is called exponentially affine

## Yields Are Affine Too

Using
$$
y_t^{(n)} = -\frac{1}{n}\log P_t^{(n)}
$$
we get
$$
y_t^{(n)}
=
-\frac{1}{n}(A_n + B_n^\top X_t)
$$

- Each maturity loads linearly on the same state vector
- The loadings vary with $n$ through $A_n$ and $B_n$
- The whole curve is one joint pricing object

## Connection Back to Lecture 17

- Diebold-Li also used a small number of factors to describe the curve [@DieboldLi2006]
- But there the loadings were chosen for fit and forecasting
- Here the loadings come from no-arbitrage restrictions [@Duffee2002; @AngPiazzesi2003]
- Most important: the model gives a disciplined $\mathbb{P}/\mathbb{Q}$ split

# Part IV: EH Component and Term Premia

## The EH Component Inside the Model

Lecture 17 defined the expectations hypothesis piece as
$$
EH_t^{(n)}
\equiv
\frac1n \sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\mathbb E_t^{\mathbb{P}}\!\left[y_{t+j}^{(1)}\right]
$$

- This is the average expected future short rate
- It is a $\mathbb{P}$-expectations object
- It is *not* computed from the bond-pricing recursion
- Here we show how to compute it once the affine model is estimated

## Forecast the State Under $\mathbb{P}$

Start from
$$
X_{t+1} = \mu + \Phi X_t + \Sigma \varepsilon_{t+1},
\qquad
\mathbb E_t^{\mathbb{P}}[\varepsilon_{t+1}] = 0
$$

Then
$$
\mathbb E_t^{\mathbb{P}}[X_{t+1}] = \mu + \Phi X_t
$$

and, recursively,
$$
\mathbb E_t^{\mathbb{P}}[X_{t+j}]
=
\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}\Phi^i \mu + \Phi^j X_t
$$

## Forecast Future Short Rates

Using
$$
y_t^{(1)} = \delta_0 + \delta_1^\top X_t
$$

we get
$$
\mathbb E_t^{\mathbb{P}}\!\left[y_{t+j}^{(1)}\right]
=
\delta_0 + \delta_1^\top \mathbb E_t^{\mathbb{P}}[X_{t+j}]
$$

So once $(\mu,\Phi,\delta_0,\delta_1)$ and $X_t$ are known,
$$
\mathbb E_t^{\mathbb{P}}\!\left[y_{t+j}^{(1)}\right]
=
\delta_0 + \delta_1^\top\left(\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}\Phi^i \mu + \Phi^j X_t\right)
$$

## Compute the EH Component

Now average those expected short rates:
$$
EH_t^{(n)}
=
\frac1n \sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\mathbb E_t^{\mathbb{P}}\!\left[y_{t+j}^{(1)}\right]
$$

Algorithm:

1. Start from the estimated state $X_t$
2. Forecast $X_{t+1},\ldots,X_{t+n-1}$ under the (model-implied) $\mathbb{P}$
3. Map each state forecast into an expected short rate
4. Average across the $n$ horizons

## Observed, Fitted, and EH Component

- Observed yield: $y_t^{(n)}$
- Fitted/model-implied yield: $\hat y_t^{(n)}$
- EH component: $EH_t^{(n)}$
- Term premium: $TP_t^{(n)}$

. . .

- In an exact-fit model, $y_t^{(n)}$ and $\hat y_t^{(n)}$ are the same
- In an estimated model with measurement error, they need not be
- But $EH_t^{(n)}$ is different from both: it uses only $\mathbb{P}$-expected short rates

## Term Premia Relative to the EH Component

In the spirit of Lecture 17, define
$$
TP_t^{(n)} = y_t^{(n)} - EH_t^{(n)}
$$

or, in an inexact-fit model,
$$
TP_t^{(n)} = \hat y_t^{(n)} - EH_t^{(n)}
$$

- This is the part of the yield not attributed to expected future short rates
- If $TP_t^{(n)}$ rises, yields rise relative to the EH component
- If $TP_t^{(n)}$ falls, yields move closer to the EH component
- This creates a gap between *observed* yields and *expected* short rates

## Why $\lambda_t$ Still Matters

- The EH component uses $\mathbb{P}$ forecasts of future short rates
- The fitted yield comes from the no-arbitrage pricing recursion
- The wedge between $\mathbb{P}$ and $\mathbb{Q}$ is driven by $\lambda_t=\lambda_0+\lambda_1 X_t$
- So $\lambda_t$ is still the key force behind time-varying term premia

# Part V: Implementation and Estimation

## Inputs After Estimation

Suppose we have estimated
$$
\mu,\ \Phi,\ \Sigma,\ \delta_0,\ \delta_1,\ \lambda_0,\ \lambda_1
$$

Then compute
$$
\mu^{\mathbb{Q}} = \mu - \Sigma\lambda_0,
\qquad
\Phi^{\mathbb{Q}} = \Phi - \Sigma\lambda_1
$$

- The fitted yield curve still uses the pricing recursion with $\mu^{\mathbb{Q}},\Phi^{\mathbb{Q}}$
- The EH component uses the $\mathbb{P}$-dynamics $(\mu,\Phi)$
- After estimation, both objects are available

## EH Component Algorithm

For each horizon $j$,
$$
\mathbb E_t^{\mathbb{P}}[X_{t+j}]
=
\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}\Phi^i \mu + \Phi^j X_t
$$

Then compute the expected future short rate:
$$
\mathbb E_t^{\mathbb{P}}\!\left[y_{t+j}^{(1)}\right]
=
\delta_0 + \delta_1^\top \mathbb E_t^{\mathbb{P}}[X_{t+j}]
$$

Finally,
$$
EH_t^{(n)}
=
\frac1n \sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\mathbb E_t^{\mathbb{P}}\!\left[y_{t+j}^{(1)}\right]
$$

## From Fitted Yields to Term Premia

1. Use the no-arbitrage recursion to compute fitted yields $\hat y_t^{(n)}$
2. Use the $\mathbb{P}$-VAR and the short-rate equation to compute $EH_t^{(n)}$
3. Define term premia as
$$
TP_t^{(n)} = \hat y_t^{(n)} - EH_t^{(n)}
$$

In an exact-fit model, this is the same as
$$
TP_t^{(n)} = y_t^{(n)} - EH_t^{(n)}
$$

## {.standout}
Questions?

## Estimation Route: Observed Factors Only

1. Choose observed factors $X_t$
2. Estimate the VAR under $\mathbb{P}$ by OLS
3. Estimate the short-rate equation
4. Choose $\lambda_0,\lambda_1$ to match the yield curve
5. Recover fitted yields, the EH component, and term premia

See also @JoslinSingletonZhu2011 and @AdrianCrumpMoench2013.

## Matching the Yield Curve

A simple objective is
$$
\min_{\lambda_0,\lambda_1}
\sum_t \sum_{n\in\mathcal M}
\left(
y_t^{(n)}-\hat y_t^{(n)}
\right)^2
$$

- $\mathcal M$: maturities used in estimation
- The $\mathbb{P}$-VAR alone is not enough
- The cross section disciplines the pricing wedge

## What the Estimated Model Delivers

- Fitted yield curves
- Risk-neutral yield curves
- Term-premium estimates by maturity and over time
- A clean separation between expected-rate news and premium news
- A bridge from term-structure data to macro and finance questions

# Part VI: A Simple Estimated DTSM

## A Simple DTSM with NS Factors

- Build $X_t=(\beta_{1t},\beta_{2t},\beta_{3t})^\top$ from a fixed-$\lambda$ Nelson-Siegel fit to the LW curve
- Monthly step; annualized continuously compounded yields
- Estimate under $\mathbb{P}$:
$$
X_{t+1} = \mu + \Phi X_t + \Sigma \varepsilon_{t+1}
$$
- Short rate and pricing wedge:
$$
y_t^{(1m)} = \delta_0 + \delta_1^\top X_t,
\qquad
\lambda_t = \lambda_0 + \lambda_1 X_t
$$
- Choose $(\lambda_0,\lambda_1)$ to fit annual maturities from 1 to 10 years

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| include: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

import time
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.dates as mdates
from scipy.optimize import minimize

plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.family": "Arial",
    "font.sans-serif": ["Arial"],
    "axes.titlesize": 15,
    "axes.labelsize": 13,
    "xtick.labelsize": 11,
    "ytick.labelsize": 11,
    "legend.fontsize": 11,
})

MATLAB_BLUE = "#0072BD"
MATLAB_ORANGE = "#D95319"
MATLAB_YELLOW = "#EDB120"

fit_start = time.perf_counter()

def ns_loadings(tau, lam):
    decay = np.exp(-lam * tau)
    slope = (1 - decay) / (lam * tau)
    curvature = slope - decay
    return np.column_stack([np.ones_like(tau), slope, curvature])

def affine_recursions(mu_q, Phi_q, Sigma, delta0, delta1, max_months):
    sigma2 = Sigma @ Sigma.T
    A = np.zeros(max_months + 1)
    B = np.zeros((max_months + 1, len(delta1)))
    for n in range(max_months):
        bn = B[n]
        A[n + 1] = A[n] + bn @ mu_q + 0.5 * bn @ sigma2 @ bn - delta0 / 12.0
        B[n + 1] = Phi_q.T @ bn - delta1 / 12.0
    return A, B

def fitted_yields(X, A, B):
    max_months = B.shape[0] - 1
    scales = -(12.0 / np.arange(1, max_months + 1))
    return (A[1:] + X @ B[1:].T) * scales

def eh_component(X, mu, Phi, delta0, delta1, n_months):
    out = np.empty(X.shape[0])
    for t in range(X.shape[0]):
        x_fore = X[t].copy()
        total = delta0 + delta1 @ x_fore
        for _ in range(1, n_months):
            x_fore = mu + Phi @ x_fore
            total += delta0 + delta1 @ x_fore
        out[t] = total / n_months
    return out

lw = pd.read_csv("../lecture17/LW_monthly.csv", skiprows=8)
lw = lw.rename(columns=lambda c: c.strip()).rename(columns={"Unnamed: 0": "date"})
lw["date"] = pd.to_datetime(lw["date"].astype(int).astype(str), format="%Y%m")

max_months = 120
curve_mats = np.arange(1, max_months + 1, dtype=float)
curve_cols = [f"{m} m" for m in range(1, max_months + 1)]
curve_sample = lw[["date"] + curve_cols].dropna(subset=curve_cols).copy()
dates_dtsm = curve_sample["date"].to_numpy()
Y = curve_sample[curve_cols].to_numpy() / 100.0

lambda_ns = 0.0609
L_ns = ns_loadings(curve_mats, lambda_ns)
X = np.linalg.lstsq(L_ns, Y.T, rcond=None)[0].T

X_t = X[:-1]
X_tp1 = X[1:]
Z = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(X_t)), X_t])
var_coef = np.linalg.lstsq(Z, X_tp1, rcond=None)[0]
mu = var_coef[0]
Phi = var_coef[1:].T
var_resid = X_tp1 - Z @ var_coef
Sigma = np.linalg.cholesky(np.cov(var_resid, rowvar=False, bias=False))

short_rate = Y[:, 0]
short_coef = np.linalg.lstsq(np.column_stack([np.ones(len(X)), X]), short_rate, rcond=None)[0]
delta0 = short_coef[0]
delta1 = short_coef[1:]

fit_mats = np.arange(12, max_months + 1, 12)
fit_idx = fit_mats - 1
Y_fit = Y[:, fit_idx]

def objective(params):
    lambda0 = params[:3]
    lambda1 = params[3:].reshape(3, 3)
    mu_q = mu - Sigma @ lambda0
    Phi_q = Phi - Sigma @ lambda1
    A, B = affine_recursions(mu_q, Phi_q, Sigma, delta0, delta1, max_months)
    yhat = fitted_yields(X, A, B)[:, fit_idx]
    return np.mean((yhat - Y_fit) ** 2)

opt = minimize(
    objective,
    np.zeros(12),
    method="L-BFGS-B",
    options={"maxiter": 200},
)

lambda0_hat = opt.x[:3]
lambda1_hat = opt.x[3:].reshape(3, 3)
mu_q = mu - Sigma @ lambda0_hat
Phi_q = Phi - Sigma @ lambda1_hat
A_hat, B_hat = affine_recursions(mu_q, Phi_q, Sigma, delta0, delta1, max_months)
fitted_curve = fitted_yields(X, A_hat, B_hat)

report_mats = {
    "1-Year": 12,
    "3-Year": 36,
    "5-Year": 60,
    "10-Year": 120,
}
eh_report = {label: eh_component(X, mu, Phi, delta0, delta1, n) for label, n in report_mats.items()}
tp_report = {label: fitted_curve[:, n - 1] - eh_report[label] for label, n in report_mats.items()}
lambda_t = (lambda0_hat[:, None] + lambda1_hat @ X.T).T

sample_start_str = curve_sample["date"].iloc[0].strftime("%Y:%m")
sample_end_str = curve_sample["date"].iloc[-1].strftime("%Y:%m")
fit_time_str = f"{time.perf_counter() - fit_start:.2f}"
```

## What We Estimate

- Data: LW monthly zero-coupon yields, balanced sample `{python} sample_start_str`--`{python} sample_end_str`
- State vector: Nelson-Siegel level, slope, and curvature with fixed $\lambda=0.0609$ [@DieboldLi2006]
- $\mathbb{P}$-dynamics: VAR(1) for the three factors
- Cross-section fit: annual maturities from 1 to 10 years
- Reported objects: observed yield, EH component, and term premium at 1y, 3y, 5y, and 10y
- Full estimation time: `{python} fit_time_str` seconds

## Actual and Fitted Yields

## Yields, EH Component, and Term Premia

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10, 5))

for ax, (label, maturity) in zip(axes.flat, report_mats.items()):
    idx = maturity - 1
    ax.plot(
        dates_dtsm,
        100 * Y[:, idx],
        color=MATLAB_BLUE,
        lw=2.0,
        label="Observed yield",
    )
    ax.plot(
        dates_dtsm,
        100 * eh_report[label],
        color=MATLAB_ORANGE,
        lw=1.8,
        label="EH component",
    )
    ax.plot(
        dates_dtsm,
        100 * tp_report[label],
        color=MATLAB_YELLOW,
        lw=1.8,
        label="Term premium",
    )
    ax.set_title(label)
    ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.YearLocator(base=10))
    ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%Y"))
    ax.grid(alpha=0.25, linewidth=0.6)
    for spine in ["top", "right"]:
        ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)

fig.supylabel("Percent")
axes[0, 0].legend(loc="upper right", frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Taking Stock

- Lecture 17 told us the curve reflects both expected rates and premia
- Lecture 18 gave a no-arbitrage model that makes that separation explicit
- $\mathbb{P}$ describes the data; $\mathbb{Q}$ prices bonds
- $\lambda_t$ is the wedge between the two
- Exponential-affine recursions turn that wedge into bond prices, yields, and term premia
